name: Leersia

project_scope.selection_mode: FINISH/ENRICH existing canonical Leersia species only
project_scope.native_zone_review: Preserve species PROVISIONAL and native_metrics_excluded fields; no BONAP/NAPA county recertification.

look_here_first: LOOK AT THE EDGES OF THE LEAVES (CAREFULLY): rice cutgrass has extremely ROUGH, backward-pointing sharp microscopic teeth on blade margins and often sheaths. In wetland stands it makes open branching panicles of small flattened grain-like one-flowered spikelets (often ~4–6 mm), with very short membranous true ligule. For L. oryzoides versus white cutgrass, compare the LOWEST panicle node (often 2 or more branches) and measured mature spikelets; do not identify by roughness alone.

recognition.where_to_look_first: A wet-edge perennial rhizomatous grass with broad rather harsh blades, panicles of narrow tiny rice-like flat spikelets, and the very short collar membrane. First photograph a margin tooth at macro scale. Then measure a single flattened spikelet, count low panicle branch number, and examine an underground rhizome only if allowed.
priority: wet creek/ditch/marsh vegetation; perennial creeping stems
blade margins strongly retrose-scabrous; avoid skin cuts
leaf sheaths often quite rough; stem nodes may have short white hair bands
slender open panicle, often 2 or more low branches per node
narrow flattened single-flowered spikelets approx 4–6.5 mm, essentially without glumes
long creeping rhizomes with loosely spaced/non-overlapping scales
recognition.field_safe_handling: Never swipe a bare finger along the sharp blade edge; use a hand lens and hold gently near the blade base.

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: SHARP LEAF EDGE + TWO LOW PANICLE BRANCHES + LONG RICE-LIKE SPIKELETS = RICE CUTGRASS CANDIDATE.
quick_split: L. oryzoides — often conspicuously VERY rough sheaths and blades, 2+ lowest panicle branches, 4–6.5mm narrow spikelets, long loosely scaled rhizomes.
L. virginica — smoother sheaths, commonly a single basal panicle branch, smaller ~2.4–4mm spikelets more overlapping along fine branches.
L. lenticularis — more lens/coin-shaped spikelets, look at exact mature outline.
Zizaniopsis miliacea — giant cutgrass, very coarse/tall; floral structure differs.
Zizania texana — Texas wild-rice, distinct endangered aquatic taxon; wet-edge foliage alone not diagnostic.
comparison_lesson.verification_rule: The broad leaf-blade hairs and roughness alone do not certify a Leersia species; images need mature spikelet, panicle node, ligule, and independent specimen confirmation.

lookalikes.field_split: Usually more delicate with smoother or only moderately rough leaf sheaths. Flowering head generally has ONE branch at a low node rather than two or more; small spikelets (~2.4–4 mm) often crowded/overlapping more strongly; short closely overlapping rhizome scales. Mature paired-branch and spikelet counts are more reliable than wet habitat alone.
lookalikes.photo_need: Whole panicle lower branching node and single spikelet with mm reference; correct source-labelled specimen.

lookalikes.field_split: Spikelets are broad and round or lens-shaped rather than elongate narrow 'rice grains'; may be nearly circular and often look like little disks. Large leaf blades may be similarly rough, so seek mature spikelet dimensions and outline.
lookalikes.photo_need: Spikelets from face and edge, with mm ruler and attached pedicel.

lookalikes.field_split: Much taller robust marsh grass with broad blades and a large branching panicle whose reproductive spikelets are organized differently; compare whole plant scale and flowering structures, not sharp leaf edges alone.
lookalikes.photo_need: Whole stand and size comparison plus panicle close-up.

lookalikes.field_split: Aquatic perennial from flowing river channels with dramatically different pollen- and seed-bearing branches. Do not mistake any narrow water-edge grass leaf for this endangered localized aquatic grass. Species diagnosis and stewardship need the actual inflorescence and habitat context.
lookalikes.photo_need: Legal non-disturbing habitat and clear flowering anatomy; never uproot protected wild-rice.

lookalikes.field_split: Many one-sided racemes bear two-flowered spikelets and a membranous ligule. Leersia typically has very rough leaf surfaces/margins, more flexible open panicle branches, and flattened one-flowered spikelets with no evident glumes.
lookalikes.photo_need: Matched leaf-edge and flowering branch + single spikelet macro.

comparison_matrix.title: Rice cutgrass versus two other cutgrasses
rows: Sharply retrorse rough margins and sheath
Usually smoother sheaths, less harsh margins
Blade margin + lower branch node + mm spikelet

what_to_teach_crew: CAREFUL: rough leaf edges are lined with tiny backward-pointing teeth that can scratch hands. Don't use your skin as a test; use a hand lens.
In the creek corridor, a broad green grass patch is not enough to identify Leersia; inspect the tiny rice-grain flowering structures.
Glumes are absent or very reduced in Leersia; don't mistake the whole flattened spikelet for one conspicuously large glume.
Try to find two or more flowering branches leaving one of the lowest panicle nodes, and compare smaller-spikeleted white cutgrass.
Most small panicle spikelets are about 4–6 mm; photograph next to a real millimeter rule, not a guessed scale.
Use source-labelled habitat photos only as context. One Joey Santore frame exists in the private study archive and has no public publishing clearance.
No range/native-metric changes from these identification lessons; field evidence is not a BONAP county certification.
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — two public-reuse source-attributed archived photos independently inspected, 6 arrow markers on visible structures; additional private video-frame excluded from public view
visual_needs: WHOLE: same rooted stand in shallow water/creek margin; multiple branches attached to base, habitat in frame.
LEAF MARGIN: strong 10× macro with 1 mm reference showing tiny DOWNWARD/RETRORSE sharp hairs or teeth; avoid running bare fingers along the edge.
TRUE LIGULE: junction of blade and sheath, roughly 0.5–1.5 mm short membranous edge with scale.
SHEATH / NODE: rough sheath surface and any small bands of hairs at attached stem nodes.
PANICLE: clearly show 2 or more branches from the LOWEST main flowering-head node, if present; contrast with white cutgrass single branch.
SPIKELET: 4–6.5 mm narrow compressed unit against millimeter scale, both faces and glume-free base/attachment shown.
RHIZOME: exposed long creeping underground stem with spaced non-overlapping scales, only where collecting is allowed; restore exposed soil.
OPTIONAL: reduced upper sheath-enclosed axillary flowerhead (cleistogamous panicle), if found on same plant.

items.label: 1 · Flattened rice-shaped spikelets against fingers
items.image_role: Source-labelled Leersia oryzoides spikelets arranged on delicate branching panicle; photographed against a hand for scale
items.caption: Many narrow flattened green spikelets are visible on thread-fine panicle stalks. This photograph establishes the overall silhouette and finger scale, not a measured 4–6 mm spikelet, the glume-free attachment point or microscopic keel hairs.
items.why_it_matters: Use this to teach what the tiny flattened spikelets look like and why a hand lens is necessary.
items.creator: Sam Kieschnick
items.photo_status: Existing local archive photo inspected visually on 2026-10-21; source determination, license shorthand/version caveat remain as originally stored.

items.label: 2 · Broad grass blades with fine open panicle
items.image_role: Source-labelled rice cutgrass with relatively broad fresh leaf blades and airy reproductive panicle held at lower center
items.caption: The image shows several broad grass blades and a delicate panicle with individual pale greenish/buff spikelets. The image DOES NOT resolve retrorse marginal teeth, ligule, hidden belowground rhizomes or exact parentage of all surrounding vegetation.
items.why_it_matters: Shows broad vegetative grass texture alongside slender branching inflorescence, but requires a fresh macro to establish cutting teeth.
items.creator: Sam Kieschnick
items.photo_status: Existing local archive image inspected 2026-10-21; original taxon identity remains source-determined, no collar or margin-teeth arrows.
